> What happens if this `<li>` does not have a parent `<ol>` nor does it have a sibiling `<li>`?

Per the sentence introducing "ordinal number", `<li>`s without parent `<ol>`s don't have ordinal numbers.

> Echoing what I said above (at the wrong location), this breaks existing browsers that treat missing default values as 0, or is this covered by the IDL reflection spec?

This does not break existing browsers because it has nothing to do with the `.value` IDL attribute. It sounds like we should add a note explicitly stating that.

body:
As @domenic noted in the issue I think I focused too much on the IDL reflection when really that doesn't come into play that much. 

1) If you're not inside an `<ol>` the value will never be used so even if these steps were followed it wouldn't result in a visible/behavioral difference? Not sure what happens then but it's outside the spec I'd think?

2) If you look at http://jsbin.com/revotubuvo/edit?html,output notice that the actual value of the ordinal of the item has nothing to do with the IDL value. True, if you set the IDL value it reflects to the attribute and affects the ordinal but inversely you can't infer what the ordinal is for an item by looking _only_ at the IDL value. If you walk through the steps here I think they give the correct results vs. implementations. You can even set the `value` to 0 or negative numbers (via `.setAttribute("value")` or the `.value` property) and they display correctly.

Ok, I see where I was wrong here. I was too fixated on the IDL stuff because the previous wording had a lot of implicit cross-references to the IDL value attribute. Reading this with fresh eyes, it's pretty clear that the IDL value attribute here only needs to reflect the value content attribute, and no other special processing is required.

I'm curious as to whether the spec for `<ol>` already defined such concepts and algorithms? If so, it may be beneficial to simply link to them instead of re-defining them here. Otherwise, LGTM.
